12. Given the basic character of the Act as a special law enacted for recovery of loans it is stressed, however, that the recovery process as prescribed in the Act nevertheless acquires a hybrid character partaking of the elements of both adversarial and non-adversarial modes of justice delivery. Submitting that the amendments of 2010 that had "drastically amended" the provisions of Section, 22, 23 and 24 can be properly understood in their true ambit and objective through the one significant single act of the omission from the law of Section 21 as previously allowed for Settlement Conferences under active judicial supervision, the petitioners in Writ Petition Nos. 6060, 6061, 8047 and 9200 of 2013 seek to establish that a comparative study of the provisions of Chapter V of the Act as stood before and after the 2010 amendments make it "crystal clear that the legislature has drastically amended the provisions of Chapter V to put mandatory obligation upon Artha Rin Court to exercise its power and adopt the procedure laid down in the said Chapter." 

 13. Citing this Court's Judgment in HMM Alam Vs. Bangladesh reported in 9 BLC (2004), 331, Mr. Sayeed aptly submits that under the pre-2010 scenario Section 21 remained distinguishable from Section 22 in that Section was clearly dependent on the will or "whims" of either party or not to pursue a resolution through Settlement Conference. The sole determinant of the availability of that avenue, this Court found was the satisfaction of the Adalat concerned dictating whether it would be fit and proper to refer the matter of Settlement Conference. The allusion of the HMM Alam Judgment to the will or "whims" of the parties distinguishably running supreme formerly under Section 22, is born out by Section 22(1) in such previous formulation reading thus subject to an all important proviso: 

 A cursory glance at the above provisions of Section 22(1) compared with the said Section's post-2010 reincarnation shows the omission of that all important proviso that was declaratory of mediation predicated upon mutual consent of the parties which once expressed would make it mandatory for the Adalat to ensure a mediated settlement. By that reason, coupled significantly with the fact of the closure wholly of the avenue of Settlement Conference under judicial supervision at the discretion of the Adalat itself, the legislature appears clearly to have strengthened the Adalat's authority under Section 22 in its revised format with a concentrated focus on the pursuit of ADR mandatory through the upgraded mode of mediation resolution. Such up gradation is evident in the simple fact that the Adalat's authority to ensure the invocation of Section 22 is now made non-derogatory. 

 21. This Court finds that the Section 22 provisions meet their limitations only in am. proceedings where clearly defendants remain absent, thereby, negating any prospects of filing written statements. Further Section. 22(1), read with Section 24(1), clearly envisages the Adalat's. auto-initiative at sending the Matter for mediation to the parties concerned and/or their appointed counsel to he facilitated, by the board of directors (BOD) of a plaintiff bank or financial institution taking preparatory steps by resolutions or decisions taken empowering a designated official to act with that process in a representative capacity. Indeed Section 24(1) does not contemplated the prospects of, and leaves no scope for, any BOD resolving not to proceed with mediation upon a referral by the Adalat under Section 22(1). There is indeed simply no avenue available to the BOD to revert to the Adalat with a negative answer in these circumstances. It is also this Court's finding that under the statutory scheme the pursuit in this context rather has to be actively of the processes spelt out in Section 22(2), (3) and (4) as progressively outline the appointment of the mediator on terms and conditions agreed upon by the parties themselves and the outcome of that exercise. Indeed Section 22(4) envisages the scenario of either failure at a mediated settlement resulting in report to be filed or, in the alternative, of that exercise meeting with success reflected in an agreement spelling out the settlement terms and conditions. 

 22. Failure at arriving at a settlement would, under Section 2(11), lead to the Adalat being obliged to revive proceedings in the suit from the stage it initially left off upon the auto-ignition of the Section 22(1) mediation process upon the filing of a written statement. It is also to be significantly noted the notwithstanding the provisions of sections 22(2) and (3), the Adalat is not relieved of its power of oversight of the mediation process and is obliged under the law to intervene in the manner dictated under Section 22(6) to itself appoint a mediator should the parties fail to do so under Section 22(3). 

 (c) in case of failure at a mediated settlement as envisaged in Section 22(1) the legislative intent is for Suit proceedings to start by reference to Section 11 of the Act onwards; 

 (d) these deductions are to be read further in conjunction with equally important provisions in Section 23 of the Act which leaves the possibility open for the parties to pursue afresh a mediated settlement subject only to the qualification that (i) this be pursued at any stage in the suit but before pronouncement of a Judgment or Order by the Adalat and, (ii) upon express prior approval of the Adalat itself. Theses conditions once fulfilled will leave it open for the parties to revisit the provision of Sections 21(2), (3) and (4) giving a mediation exercise a second lease in life; and 

 (e) it follows that the jurisdictional distinction between Section 22(1) and 23(1) notably is that it is only in the latter instance that the will of the parties becomes an important factor in initiating the second renewed phase at mediation. That subjective element is notably wholly absent in Section 22(1). In fact this serves as a notice on the parties to take the initial exercise at a mediated settlement under Section 22 very seriously and not to be whimsical and cavalier about it given that a renewed attempt at such a mediated settlement is contingent on the all important factor of the approval of the Adalat. Should that approval not be forthcoming the parties can only lament about a missed opportunity under Section 22. From another perspective, Section 23 reiterates and fortifies the Act's scheme reflected in Section 22 being that of primacy of consideration to be given by the Adalat and the parties to ensure a mediated settlement of claim at the very first opportunity without any exception. 

 However, that delicate balance, by practice or otherwise, has given way to a noticeable imbalance over the years tipping the scale disproportionately in favour of claimant banks and financial institutions. This is plainly due to an overly misconceived reliance on the Section 33 provisions of the Act in preference to the other provisions aiming at a conciliatory settlement of dispute chiefly under Sections 22, 23 and 24 of the Act and equally significantly under Sections 38, 45, 49 and 57 of the Act. 

 27. It is in that context that this Court has especially directed the learned Deputy Attorney General Mr. Md. Shahidul Islam and the learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Sukumar Biswas to ensure a special service of this Judgment and Order on the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for urgent and necessary consideration and action. It remains the concern of this Court that the Act be understood and applied with utmost precision and accuracy by all Joint District Judges assigned to preside over the Artha Rin Adalat if only to give primacy to avenues of ADR that have gained prominence in terms of legislative policy and governmental action over the past many years. It is this Court's firm belief that an orientation in and the understanding of the Act has become necessary now and should this go unaddressed a crisis of some magnitude will be in the offing in which the Act risks degenerating into a vehicle of exploitation and undue hardship. Clearly, the legislators never meant to be so unkind even to an alleged defaulter. The learned Deputy Attorney General and Assistant Attorney General as Officers of this Court shall duly apprise this Court, as necessary, of active steps taken by the concerned Ministry and/or its relevant Wing and Department , to so restore the balance between the adversarial and non-adversarial; mode of loan recovery envisaged in the Act bearing in mind the views and considerations reflected in this Judgment and Order. That being a relatively long-term outlook, in the more immediate future the Adalat in each instance shall now be expected of its own volition and authority to invoke Section 22 of the Act and refer the parties to actively seek a mediated settlements in keeping with the mandatory provisions of Chapter V of the Act. That shall indeed be true of all the seven Writ Petitions before us. Accordingly, it shall be incumbent upon the Adalat in each of these cases to forthwith, at its own initiative, start the mediation process and see that process through strictly in accordance with the Section 22 prescriptions and Chapter V provisions of the Act.
